Notes: The Old Swedish Ræfla is corresponded by Reuele in the Low Middle German version of Consolation of the Soul (Henning 1954: 426). According to Eesti kohanimeraamat the historical name of Tallinn, Reval, and its variants Räväl, Rävul, Rääveli go back to the name of the surrounding county. There is no consensus regarding the etymological provenance of the name. According to one line of argumentation, the name is associated with the Estonian village name Räbala : Rebala meaning 'strip of land', cf. the words räbal : ribal. There is however another hypothesis linking the place name Rebala with the word reba meaning 'fox'. Scandinavians are assumed to have re-shaped the name to Ræfla and similar forms due to folk etymological associations with the words rev 'reef' and revel : rävla 'beam; balk'.  Furthermore, the dictionary of Old Swedish, Söderwall's Ordbok öfver svenska medeltids-språket (1884–1973), includes two relevant entries, ræflisker adj. 'of Reval', and ræfflisa f. 'woman from Reval'. Based on this information, the Norse World project normalises the Old Swedish lemma form as Ræfla.

Original form: Oc wi kommom skøt i en skogh som kallas sancti marthens skogh
Standard form: Sancti Martini skogher, Sankte Martens skogher
Notes: Sancti Martini skogher/Sankte Martens skogher is attested as sancti marthens skogh in A 49, and sancti martini skogh in D 4. In A 49 it says: Oc wi kommom skøt i en skogh som kallas sancti marthens skogh ‘And we came soon to a forest that is called the Forest of Saint Martin’. It appears to be situated around one day’s travel from Rome, based on the context of the story. It is referred to as a skogher ‘forest’. In D 4, the son of the emperor tells the wise men: J skulin wara nær i stadhin som heter sancti martini skogh ‘you will be close at the place/city that is called the Forest of Saint Martin’, where close in a pragmatic sense means ‘close to him in Rome’. Here it is not referred to as a skogher, but a staþer, which means both ‘place’ and ‘city’. The former meaning is perhaps more likely. It is after all named sancti martini skogh.  We therefore interpret Sancti Martini skogher/Sankte Martens skogher in both of these attestations to denote a forest in the vicinity of Rome. Even though the context differs somewhat, it seems to correspond to Sancti Macius hovuþstaþer in AM 191 fol., which obviously refers to a city. In the Old French version of Sju vise mästare Saint-Martin is both the name of a town close to Constantinople and two churches (Misrahi 1933, p. 141). In the Middle English version it says: þat gardyne þat was kald Boys Saynt Martine. It is in other words a garden, but boys is Middle English (from Old French) and means ‘grove, woods’. Killis Campbell asks himself whether it is ”possible that the name is, after all, to be traced to the Campus Martius” in Rome, due to confusion of Mars and St. Martin (1907, p. 16, 155). Notes: According to Sturekrönikorna (Sture's Chronicles) in the manuscript Stockholm, National Library of Sweden, D 5, the regent Charles VIII of Sweden went to exile in Gdansk (Danzig) in Prussia where he later received the so-called Puske rinchil as a pawn. Traditionally, it is assumed that Charles VIII of Sweden came into possession of the city of Puck (Putzig; spelled Bautzig, Pautzke, Putzc etc in the Middle Ages) and its lands in the vicinity of Gdansk. However, the manuscript form of the place name, Puske rinchil, suggests a somewhat different location. Perhaps, the word rinchil could be interpreted as a misspelling of rinnil 'small flow', a derivate from the verb rinna 'run; flow', but this is not certain. Or it could be a scribal error: the v or w in winkel has been read as an r, so *vinkil became rinchil. We use the coordinates of the city of Puck (Putzig) to visualise Zatoka Pucka (Putziger Wiek or Putziger Winkel).

Notes: Based primarily on the geographical context of the story and comments in the preface, Gustav Storm (1877) has argued that Hunaland, Attila’s kingdom, in the case of Didrik av Bern, denotes Saxony. Didrik av Bern – i.e. the prose versions preserved in the Scandinavian sources – is a translation of Saxon stories (or a story), in which the geographical context has been moved from southern Germany, from where the story originates. In the south German poetic versions Hunaland denotes Hungary according to Storm 1877, p. 329. However, Hunaland should not be seen as a name of Saxony itself, since the name Saxony actually exists in the story: Sassen. Consequently, hyner cannot mean ‘Saxons’. Preferably, Hunaland should be seen as a fictional country of the past. In an etymological sense, however, Hunaland is of course the country of the Huns, i.e. the notorious nomadic tribe of the Migration Period. Hunaland is shown as Soest (Old Swedish Susa) on the map, since it is Attila’s residence in Didrik av Bern.   Storm, Gustav, 1877: Nye Studier over Thidreks Saga. In: Aarbøger for nordisk oldkyndighed og historie. Notes: According to Eesti kohanimeraamat the historical name of Tallinn, Reval, and its variants Räväl, Rävul, Rääveli go back to the name of the surrounding county. There is no consensus regarding the etymological provenance of the name. According to one line of argumentation, the name is associated with the Estonian village name Räbala : Rebala meaning 'strip of land', cf. the words räbal : ribal. There is however another hypothesis linking the place name Rebala with the word reba meaning 'fox'. Scandinavians are assumed to have re-shaped the name to Ræfla and similar forms due to folk etymological associations with the words rev 'reef' and revel : rävla 'beam; balk'.  Furthermore, the dictionary of Old Swedish, Söderwall's Ordbok öfver svenska medeltids-språket (1884–1973), includes two relevant entries, ræflisker adj. 'of Reval', and ræfflisa f. 'woman from Reval'. Based on this information, the Norse World project normalises the Old Swedish lemma form as Ræfla.

In the south German poetic versions Hunaland denotes Hungary according to Storm 1877, p. 329. However, Hunaland should not be seen as a name of Saxony itself, since the name Saxony actually exists in the story: Sassen. Consequently, hyner cannot mean ‘Saxons’. Preferably, Hunaland should be seen as a fictional country of the past. In an etymological sense, however, Hunaland is of course the country of the Huns, i.e. the notorious nomadic tribe of the Migration Period. Hunaland is shown as Soest (Old Swedish Susa) on the map, since it is Attila’s residence in Didrik av Bern.   Storm, Gustav, 1877: Nye Studier over Thidreks Saga. In: Aarbøger for nordisk oldkyndighed og historie. Original form: hwre storan skada han haffde fongit aff konungen i wilcina land.
Notes: Vilkinaland is the land of the vilkina mæn. The name originates from the Slavic tribe Veleti, German Wilzen, but it is identified as Sweden in Didrik av Bern, e.g. vilkinia landh som nw kallas swerige. Instead he believes it was used by the Saxons as a common name for their pagan enemies of the north and east.     Storm, Gustav, 1877: Nye Studier over Thidreks Saga. In: Aarbøger for nordisk oldkyndighed og historie. Notes: Humlungaland is the country of the humlungar in the story. It corresponds to Amlungaland (Aum-/Øm-/Ør/Hum-) in the Old West Norse sources (Bertelsen 1905–11 II, p. 400). ok kom til eth vaptn som møre heth
Notes: Møre in Didrik av Bern is a lake (vatn, sior) connected with the Rhine, where Hagen meets and kills two mermaids. The name could, perhaps, have a connection with Moeringen (modern-day Großmehring in Ingolstadt) in Nibelungenlied, the place where Hagen leads the Burgundians (Nibelungs) over the Danube (see Paff 1959, p. 132 ff.). A Study in Germanic Heroic Legend.

Notes: Hunaland is the land of the hyner.  Based primarily on the geographical context of the story and comments in the preface, Gustav Storm (1877) has argued that Hunaland, Attila’s kingdom, in the case of Didrik av Bern, denotes Saxony. Preferably, Hunaland should be seen as a fictional country of the past. In an etymological sense, however, Hunaland is of course the country of the Huns, i.e. the notorious nomadic tribe of the Migration Period.   Storm, Gustav, 1877: Nye Studier over Thidreks Saga. In: Aarbøger for nordisk oldkyndighed og historie. Original form: oc haffde medh sik allan hunaher.
Notes: Hunaland is the land of the hyner.  Based primarily on the geographical context of the story and comments in the preface, Gustav Storm (1877) has argued that Hunaland, Attila’s kingdom, in the case of Didrik av Bern, denotes Saxony. Didrik av Bern – i.e. the prose versions preserved in the Scandinavian sources – is a translation of Saxon stories (or a story), in which the geographical context has been moved from southern Germany, from where the story originates. In the south German poetic versions Hunaland denotes Hungary according to Storm 1877, p. 329. However, Hunaland should not be seen as a name of Saxony itself, since the name Saxony actually exists in the story: Sassen. Consequently, hyner cannot mean ‘Saxons’. Preferably, Hunaland should be seen as a fictional country of the past. In an etymological sense, however, Hunaland is of course the country of the Huns, i.e. the notorious nomadic tribe of the Migration Period.   Storm, Gustav, 1877: Nye Studier over Thidreks Saga. In: Aarbøger for nordisk oldkyndighed og historie. P. 297–346.

Original form: ok loth bæra baner før sik mith j vilcinia her /
Notes: The first element can be interpreted as a Latin place-name formation with -ia.  The attestation vilcinia her is categorized under the standard form vilkina man. Compare that huna hær has the standard form Hun, ryze hertoghen has Russian etc. Vilkinaland is the land of the vilkina mæn. The name originates from the Slavic tribe Veleti, German Wilzen, but it is identified as Sweden in Didrik av Bern, e.g. vilkinia landh som nw kallas swerige. But it is clear that Vilkinaland and Sverige can also denote different referents, e.g. han wan medh stridh wilcina land. som nw ær kalladh swerige oc gøtaland. oc skane oc siæland oc winland oc all the rike ther till lage. It is thus included in Norse World. Gustav Storm concludes that a big, united Vilkinaland of Slavic and North Germanic tribes probably never existed (1877 p. 341). Instead he believes it was used by the Saxons as a common name for their pagan enemies of the north and east.     Storm, Gustav, 1877: Nye Studier over Thidreks Saga. In: Aarbøger for nordisk oldkyndighed og historie. P. 297–346.

Notes: The identification of the Old Swedish place name Kapiferi is unclear. According to Klemming, the Old Swedish version of the Alexander legend goes back to one of the redactions of Incipit liber Alexandri Magni regis Macedoniae de preliis by the Neapolitan Archpresbyter Leo. In other versions of the legend, including Leo's text, the city where Alexander receives a prophecy of his early death is named Taphosiris : Taphosiri : Tafosiri : Taforisis (Historia Alexandri Magni 1472; Budge 1889; Bergmerister 1975: 48a–49b etc.). The location can thus possibly be linked to Taposiris Magna. However, it should be noted that Kapiferi placed in Africa in Konung Alexander (The Romance of Alexander the Great) is not referred to as a city in the Swedish text; the information on the type of location is thus supplied from other sources. It is likely that the form Kapiferi came about as a result of copyists' mistakes in several stages; the letters ⟨c⟩ and ⟨t⟩ as well as the so-called tall ⟨s⟩ and ⟨f⟩ looked very much alike, which could lead to misspellings. Original form: thy kretis folk kunno medh lista | the fughla fa før the aff wisto
Notes: The possible inhabitant designation kretis folk 'Creti's people' is attested in the Old Swedish Konung Alexander (The Romance of Alexander the Great). The kretis folk are said to capture and consume the many birds that inhabited Skaloniahedh (Skalonia Heath) where Alexandria was founded. The episode has a parallel in the Orosius recension of the Incipit liber Alexandri Magni regis Macedoniae de preliis by the Neapolitan Archpresbyter Leo or J2 according to Bergmeister (1975: 53b). However, kretis folk seems to be a misinterpretation of the Latin word creta 'clay', cf. Cui cum architectus Dinocrates nomine casu accidente ibi non esset, sed tamen in creta fundande urbis fana fixit. Ubi infinite aves convolaverunt et in circuitu crete sederunt et comederunt eam. It is of course not possible to know what kind of people the Swedish translator had in mind. There are at least two possible indentifications of the inhabitant designation in the Old Swedish text. The kretis folk can either be linked to the Biblical people of kreti 'Cherethites' or to the inhabitants of the island of Crete. The visualisation of the spatial reference employed in the Norse World resource relies on the fact that the inhabitant designation is linked to a location in the vicinity of Alexandria in Egypt. Notes: The Old Swedish Konung Alexander (The Romance of Alexander the Great) mentions two cities that belong to Tyrians, Cecilia and Rodis. Alexander destroys them and then continues to Jerusalem. The episode has a parallel in the Orosius recension of the Incipit liber Alexandri Magni regis Macedoniae de preliis by the Neapolitan Archpresbyter Leo or J2 according to Bergmeister (1975: 63b). However, the two corresponding locations referred to in the Latin texts are the islands of Sicily and Rhodes, not two fictive cities, cf. "Deinde Ciliciam et Rodum crudeli furore pervadens veniensque ad civitatem Iherosolimam ascendere festinabat." In the Norse World resource, we use the information in the original source as a point of departure for visualising the material. Thus, both fictive cities are visualised as located in Lebanon.
